summary.text: The proof uses \(n=736\): since every base in a putative representation is at most \(\lfloor\sqrt{736}\rfloor=27\), it exhaustively rules out sums of one, two, three, or four nondecreasing squares whose smallest base is at least \(8\). Thus \(a(736)\le 7\), while \(736>599\), giving the counterexample.

full_proof.text:
For a positive integer \(n\), let \(L(n)\) be the set of positive integers \(k\) for which there is a representation
\[
n=x_1^2+\cdots+x_r^2,
\qquad 1\le r\le 4,
\qquad 0<x_1\le x_2\le\cdots\le x_r,
\]
whose least base is \(x_1=k\). The sequence value \(a(n)\) is the largest member of \(L(n)\). (Every base in such a representation is at most \(\sqrt n\), so this set is finite; the four-square theorem ensures that it is nonempty. For the particular integer used below, nonemptiness will also follow from an explicit representation.)

We disprove the assertion that \(a(n)>7\) for every \(n>599\) by taking
\[
n=736.
\]
Certainly \(736>599\). We will prove that every representation of \(736\) as a sum of at most four positive squares has least base at most \(7\). It will then follow immediately that \(a(736)\le 7\), contradicting the conjectured strict inequality.

First, the set of representations under consideration is indeed nonempty, since
\[
736=4^2+12^2+24^2=16+144+576.
\]
There is also the representation
\[
736=4^2+8^2+16^2+20^2,
\]
but only one explicit representation is needed for nonemptiness.

Suppose, toward a contradiction, that \(736\) has a representation by at most four positive squares whose least base is at least \(8\). After arranging the bases in nondecreasing order, write it as
\[
736=x_1^2+\cdots+x_r^2,
\qquad 1\le r\le4,
\qquad 8\le x_1\le\cdots\le x_r.
\]
Thus every \(x_i\) is at least \(8\).

We first make a modular reduction that sharply limits the possible parities of the bases. The possible square residues modulo \(16\) are
\[
0,1,4,9.
\]
More precisely, a square is congruent to \(0\pmod {16}\) exactly when its base is divisible by \(4\), and it is congruent to \(4\pmod {16}\) exactly when its base is even but not divisible by \(4\), that is, when the base is congruent to \(2\pmod4\). Since
\[
736=46\cdot16\equiv0\pmod {16},
\]
the residues of the \(r\) squares must add to \(0\pmod {16}\).

For completeness, checking all multisets of at most four elements from \(\{0,1,4,9\}\) gives the following complete list of those whose sum is \(0\pmod {16}\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{number of squares}&\text{possible multiset of square residues}\cr
\hline
1&\{0\},\cr
2&\{0,0\},\cr
3&\{0,0,0\},\cr
4&\{0,0,0,0\}\text{ or }\{4,4,4,4\}.
\end{array}
\]
This small residue table is exhaustive because each square has one of the four displayed residues; direct addition shows that no other multiset of the relevant size has sum divisible by \(16\).

We now eliminate each possible number \(r\) of squares.

**Case 1: \(r=1\).**

The residue table says that \(x_1\) is divisible by \(4\). Write \(x_1=4X\). Dividing \(x_1^2=736\) by \(16\) gives
\[
X^2=46.
\]
This is impossible, since
\[
6^2=36<46<49=7^2.
\]

**Case 2: \(r=2\).**

Both bases are divisible by \(4\), so write
\[
x_1=4X,\qquad x_2=4Y.
\]
After division by \(16\), the equation becomes
\[
X^2+Y^2=46.
\]
Modulo \(8\), a square can only be \(0\), \(1\), or \(4\). Consequently, a sum of two squares can have only one of the residues
\[
0,1,2,4,5\pmod8:
\]
these come from adding two elements of \(\{0,1,4\}\). But \(46\equiv6\pmod8\), which is not on this list. Hence this case is impossible.

**Case 3: \(r=3\).**

Again all three bases are divisible by \(4\). Put
\[
x_1=4X,\qquad x_2=4Y,\qquad x_3=4Z.
\]
Because \(x_1\ge8\) and the bases are nondecreasing, we have
\[
2\le X\le Y\le Z.
\]
Dividing the original equation by \(16\) gives
\[
X^2+Y^2+Z^2=46.
\]
Since \(X\le Y\le Z\),
\[
3X^2\le X^2+Y^2+Z^2=46.
\]
Together with \(X\ge2\), this forces \(X=2\) or \(X=3\).

If \(X=2\), then
\[
Y^2+Z^2=42.
\]
Reducing modulo \(8\), the right side is \(2\). Among square residues \(0,1,4\pmod8\), the only way for two of them to sum to \(2\pmod8\) is \(1+1\). Thus both \(Y\) and \(Z\) are odd. Also, because \(Y\le Z\),
\[
2Y^2\le Y^2+Z^2=42,
\]
so \(Y^2\le21\) and hence \(Y\le4\). The conditions \(Y\ge2\), \(Y\le4\), and \(Y\) odd force \(Y=3\). The equation would then give
\[
Z^2=42-9=33,
\]
which is impossible because \(5^2=25<33<36=6^2\).

If \(X=3\), then
\[
Y^2+Z^2=37.
\]
Again using \(Y\le Z\), we obtain \(2Y^2\le37\). Since also \(Y\ge X=3\), this leaves only \(Y=3\) or \(Y=4\). For \(Y=3\), one gets \(Z^2=28\), which lies strictly between \(5^2=25\) and \(6^2=36\). For \(Y=4\), one gets \(Z^2=21\), which lies strictly between \(4^2=16\) and \(5^2=25\). Neither is a square. Thus a three-square representation with all bases at least \(8\) is impossible.

**Case 4: \(r=4\).**

The modulo-\(16\) table gives two subcases.

First suppose all four square residues are \(0\pmod {16}\). Then every base is divisible by \(4\). Write
\[
x_1=4X,\quad x_2=4Y,\quad x_3=4Z,\quad x_4=4W.
\]
The ordering and lower bound give
\[
2\le X\le Y\le Z\le W,
\]
and division by \(16\) gives
\[
X^2+Y^2+Z^2+W^2=46.
\]
We show directly that four squares of integers at least \(2\) cannot sum to \(46\).

Modulo \(8\), the four square residues, each belonging to \(\{0,1,4\}\), must sum to
\[
46\equiv6\pmod8.
\]
The only multiset of four elements from \(\{0,1,4\}\) with sum congruent to \(6\pmod8\) is
\[
\{0,1,1,4\}.
\]
Indeed, direct addition of the possible residue multisets gives this unique pattern. Thus, among \(X,Y,Z,W\), one has square residue \(0\pmod8\), two have square residue \(1\pmod8\), and one has square residue \(4\pmod8\).

An integer whose square is \(0\pmod8\) is divisible by \(4\). Since its square is one of four nonnegative summands totaling \(46\), this integer can only be \(4\): the next positive multiple of \(4\), namely \(8\), already has square \(64>46\). The integer whose square is \(4\pmod8\) is congruent to \(2\pmod4\). It cannot be \(6\) or larger, because its square would then be at least \(36\), and together with the square \(4^2=16\) already identified the total would exceed \(46\). Since all four integers are at least \(2\), this integer must therefore be \(2\).

The remaining two integers are odd and at least \(2\), hence at least \(3\). Their squares must satisfy
\[
U^2+V^2=46-4^2-2^2=26.
\]
Any such odd integer whose square does not exceed \(26\) is either \(3\) or \(5\). The possible sums of two corresponding odd squares are
\[
3^2+3^2=18,\qquad 3^2+5^2=34,\qquad 5^2+5^2=50,
\]
none of which is \(26\). This eliminates the first four-square subcase.

It remains to consider the residue pattern \(\{4,4,4,4\}\). Here each \(x_i^2\equiv4\pmod {16}\), so each base is congruent to \(2\pmod4\). We may therefore write
\[
x_i=2u_i
\]
with every \(u_i\) odd. Dividing
\[
x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2+x_4^2=736
\]
by \(4\) gives
\[
u_1^2+u_2^2+u_3^2+u_4^2=184.
\]
Every odd square is congruent to \(1\pmod8\), so the left side is congruent to \(4\pmod8\). The right side, however, satisfies \(184\equiv0\pmod8\). This contradiction eliminates the second subcase.

We have exhausted all possibilities \(r=1,2,3,4\). Therefore there is no representation of \(736\) as a sum of at most four positive squares in which every base is at least \(8\). Equivalently, in every such representation, the least base is at most \(7\). Hence every member of \(L(736)\) is at most \(7\), and consequently
\[
a(736)=\max L(736)\le7.
\]
Since \(736>599\), this single value contradicts the proposed assertion that \(a(n)>7\) for every \(n>599\). Thus the conjecture is false.
